extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners and scholars (patent drafters, litigators, judges, and academics)
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing and drafting patent claims with attention to element-definition (granularity) to maximize notice-quality and litigation-resistance, and to anticipate Doctrine of Equivalents and Markman outcomes. The rubric applies to evaluating issued patents or guiding claim drafting/prosecution strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Element-granularity choice (coarse vs. fine)
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim construer’s choice of element granularity (coarse parsing into few multi-word elements vs. fine parsing into many single-word/short-phrase elements) decisively affects claim scope: coarse parsing yields broader doctrine-of-equivalents reach and broader literal scope; fine parsing yields narrower literal scope and more opportunities to defeat equivalence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no neutral or correct granularity; the choice depends on the construer’s purposes. Drafting is strategic: broad elements increase DOE reach but raise indefiniteness and 112(f) risks; narrow elements reduce DOE reach but support defensible literal scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit element boundaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the element boundaries marked explicitly (commas, structural separators, 'comprising' introduction)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use punctuation and structural markers in claim language to make element boundaries explicit. Clear boundaries reduce claim-construction uncertainty and limit unexpected parsing variations during Markman.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification vocabulary maps to claim elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the specification consistently use vocabulary that maps to claim elements?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent, element-defining vocabulary in the specification supports a predictable mapping from claim language to disclosed structure/function. Inconsistent or varied terminology invites divergent constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Working/examples illustrating each element
rubrics_metrics.description: Are there working examples illustrating each claim element?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide examples in the specification that demonstrate and instantiate claimed elements; examples help courts identify element boundaries and support desired granularity in claim construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution history reflects consistent element granularity
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the prosecution history reflect a consistent element granularity (i.e., did the applicant commit to a particular parsing during prosecution)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prosecution statements that consistently treat elements support that granularity at Markman. Inconsistent or opportunistic prosecution arguments create ambiguity and risk unpredictable interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent claims reinforce independent claim parsing
rubrics_metrics.description: Are dependent claims structured to reinforce (not contradict) the independent claim's element parsing?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft dependent claims so they clarify and narrow elements in ways consistent with the independent claim’s element boundaries; avoid dependent claims that imply alternate parsing or combine/disaggregate elements in conflicting ways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of bracketed/numbered limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of bracketed/numbered limitations in claim language to increase notice-quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bracketed or numbered limitations make element boundaries visually and structurally clear, aiding notice to competitors and promoting predictable claim construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defined claim terms for novel or coined vocabulary
rubrics_metrics.description: Are novel or coined claim terms expressly defined in the specification?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defining novel or coined terms in the specification reduces ambiguity and prevents later parties from pressing conflicting constructions that alter element granularity or scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid run-on element descriptions and lumping concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality defects include run-on element descriptions that blur boundaries, and single phrases that combine multiple distinct concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid long, multi-concept phrases that make it unclear how many elements there are or what each element covers. Break distinct functional/structural concepts into discrete, clearly signposted limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: No conflicting element interpretations across embodiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Are there conflicting element interpretations suggested by different embodiments in the specification?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure embodiments consistently reflect the same element parsing. Conflicting uses across embodiments invite courts to adopt unpredictable granularities or to read elements as optional/variable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment of asserted Doctrine-of-Equivalents (DOE) reach with granularity strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: What is the asserted DOE reach, and does it match the element-granularity strategy (broad elements = broader DOE reach; narrow elements = narrower DOE reach)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drafting strategy should consciously choose between broad functional element formulations (to maximize DOE) and narrow structural formulations (to maximize literal defensibility), while accounting for risks like indefiniteness and 112(f).

rubrics_metrics.name: Element granularity’s impact on Function-Way-Result (FWR) DOE test
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the chosen element granularity facilitate or impede FWR analysis (function, way, result) for accusing products?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coarse-element analyses make FWR identity easier to find; fine-element analyses make it harder. Provide specification support for the granularity you intend so courts can properly apply FWR prongs at the chosen level of analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operative element-definition test (five-point checklist)
rubrics_metrics.description: A five-question operative test to assess element-definition quality: (1) Are element boundaries marked explicitly? (2) Does the specification consistently use vocabulary mapping to claim elements? (3) Are there working examples illustrating each element? (4) Does the prosecution history reflect a consistent element granularity? (5) Are dependent claims structured to reinforce the independent claim's element parsing?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents passing all five tests have predictable claim construction; failing them increases Markman risk. Use this checklist to evaluate issued patents or to guide drafting and prosecution.
